sentences.text: Colle and Fonte are eleven hundred metres apart across a wooded ridge in the Abruzzo and there is no road between them.
There was a road.

It went over the top and it was a mule track that had been a mule track since the Romans, and it is still there under about fifty years of hornbeam and it is perfectly walkable if you know it, and Dario has walked it, and he is not supposed to have.
The road that exists now goes down from Colle to the valley and along and back up to Fonte and it is twenty-nine kilometres and takes fifty minutes.
Nobody makes that drive.

That is the thing to understand about the geography: it is not that the two villages are far apart, it is that they are eleven hundred metres apart and might as well be in different countries, and the fifty minutes exists as a fact and has almost never been used.
Dario has been to Fonte twice in his life.
Once at seven, for a funeral of somebody related through a marriage in the 1950s, in a car, with his mother, without his grandfather.
And once at nineteen.
The thing that happened in 1974 was about water.
Dario would like to set out the whole of it, because everybody assumes it must have been something enormous.

There is a spring on the Colle side of the ridge and it had fed both villages through a masonry channel since 1911, and in 1972 the comune of Colle put in a new tank and the channel was cut, and it was almost certainly not deliberate — the men who did it were from Pescara and they were laying a pipe — and Fonte was without water for eleven days in the August.
There was a meeting.
It went badly.
There was a second meeting that went worse, and there was a court case that ran until 1979 and that Fonte won, and by then it was not about water.
Dario has read the judgment.

It is in the comune archive at Colle and it is fourteen pages and it is extremely boring, and the operative part is about who owns a masonry channel built in 1911 under an agreement that nobody could produce.
Fonte got the water back in the September of 1972, eleven days after it stopped.
The whole of the actual problem lasted a week and a half.
Dario's grandfather has not spoken to anybody from Fonte since he was twenty-two.
He has spoken to people from Fonte.
Dario has watched him do it — at a hospital in Sulmona, at a market, once at a wedding — perfectly civilly, about the weather, for two minutes at a time.
What he has not done in fifty-one years is have a conversation.
He is not a bitter man.
That is the part Dario has never got anybody outside the valley to understand.

He tried it once on a girlfriend from Rome, who said, reasonably, that it sounded as though everybody should get over it, and Dario found that he could not construct a single sentence in his grandfather's defence and also could not agree with her.

He is a cheerful, decent, extremely funny old man who has three friends in the valley and goes to everything and helps everybody, and if you say the word Fonte at his table the temperature goes down four degrees and stays there for the rest of the meal.
